pamphlet_excerpts: At least two sources of weather: The first weather satellite, known as TIROS-1, waslaunched in the spring of 1960 (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 2: It was highly successfulat giving meteorologists their first overall view of entirestorm systems (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 3: Since then, satellites have become muchmore sophisticated, allowing a nearly continuous watchover the entire Earth (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 4: NOAA has two satellite systems: polar-orbiting satellites and geostationary satellites (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (At least two sources of weather): The satellite systems are named Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES) and Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (p. 33).
Step 2 (At least two sources of weather): The polar-orbiting satellites circle Earth, passingover or near the poles at a height of approximately 520 miles (p. 33).
Step 3 (At least two sources of weather): Theytravel around the globe several times each day (p. 33).
Step 4 (At least two sources of weather): The polar-orbitingsatellites are placed in sun-synchronous orbits, which means theypass over the same spot at the same time each day (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps: Recall that weather is the condition of the atmosphere over aparticular area for a short time (p. 66).
Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 2: Climate is the average of theweather over a region for a longer time, such as 30 years (p. 66).

Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 3: The word climate comes from the Greek word klima, meaning "angle." This name was used because the angle atwhich the sun strikes Earth largely determines (p. 66).
Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 4: At the equator, the sun is nearly straight overhead most of the year, so most of the equatorial region is hot (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): Poleward from the equator, theclimate gradually shifts from hot to cold (p. 66).
Step 2 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): This tilt (about 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular) remains the same allyear as seen from deep space (top) but changes relative to the sun (p. 66).
Step 3 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): At thesummer solstice (the first day of summer, bottom left), the North Pole tilts toward thesun, and the sun reaches its northernmost point (p. 66).
Step 4 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): This is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere (p. 66).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Make one of the following instruments: wind vane, anemometer, rain gauge, or hygrometer. Keep a daily weather log for one week using information from this instrument as well as from other sources such as local radio and television stations, NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards, and internet sources (with your parent or guardian's permission). Record the following information at the same time every day: wind direction and speed, temperature, precipitation, and types of clouds. Be sure to make a note of any morning dew or frost. In the log, also list the weather forecasts from radio or television at the same time each day and show how the weather really turned out. (b) Visit a National Weather Service office or talk with a local radio or television weathercaster, private meteorologist, local agricultural extension service officer, or university meteorology instructor. Find out what type of weather is most dangerous or damaging to your community. Determine how severe weather and flood warnings reach the homes in your community.

pamphlet_excerpts: Talk of At Least Five: Give A Talk: Although lightning can be hazardous, it is not all bad (p. 37).
Talk of At Least Five Principle 2: Give A Talk Principle 2: It changes theair's nitrogen into a form that can be taken up byplants (p. 37).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Talk of At Least Five): Step 1 (Give A Talk): Becauselightning follows the path of leastresistance, objects closer to the cloud are more likely to be struck (p. 37).
Step 2 (Talk of At Least Five): Step 2 (Give A Talk): Trees inan otherwise open space often aretargets for lightning, so trees arenot a good place to take shelter in a thunderstorm (p. 37).
Step 3 (Talk of At Least Five): Step 3 (Give A Talk): Thunderstorms can becomequite violent, producing large hail, flooding rains, strong winds, andtornadoes (p. 37).
Step 4 (Talk of At Least Five): Step 4 (Give A Talk): These severe thunderstorms tend to occur where the air mass is very unstable (p. 37).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: The meteorologists you probably are most familiar with are the weather newscasters on television (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: But there are manyadditional career opportunities for meteorologists (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Such researchers work for universities, privateindustry, and the U. S. government (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is just one governmentagency that uses researchers (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Many researchers analyze levels of pollution in the oceans and atmosphere (p. 61).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): At the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), climate research is ahigh priority (p. 61).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): At universities, meteorology professors teach andconduct research (p. 61).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Their research is usually supported by grants from the government or private foundations (p. 61).
